Introduction
My first ONNX helper class for this article failed in a way I did not see at first. It created the session, set the input shape, and called OnnxRun() with one buffer for the predicted label. The model was a scikit-learn pipeline with two outputs, the label and the class probabilities. So every call failed with error 5804, and the journal said "incorrect parameters count passed to OnnxRun, expected 3 instead of 2". My own test script then reported 50 rows with 0 matches and 0 mismatches, and still printed PASS. The model was fine. The code around it was wrong, and the test could not tell.
That mistake changed the topic of the article. Exporting a model to ONNX is well covered on MQL5. I did not find a set of checks for an EA to run in OnInit before its first prediction. So I wrote three classes and a Python tool:
COnnxContract compares a model with a small contract file. The file lists the inputs and outputs the code expects, the feature order, the class labels, and the SHA-256 of the model file.
COnnxClassifier loads a classifier only if it passes that check, and gives OnnxRun() a buffer for every output.
COnnxParity runs a golden file through the terminal and compares every probability with the answer onnxruntime gave in Python for the same row.
The script make_check_files.py writes the contract and the golden file for a classifier exported with zipmap off, from your own rows. It can also audit the log an EA writes while it runs.
The checks answer different questions. The hash shows whether the file is byte for byte the one the contract was written for. The signature check shows whether the code can call the model at all. The golden file shows whether the terminal computes the same numbers as onnxruntime on the rows in that file. None of them says whether the model is any good, and the golden file says nothing about rows outside it.
I tested the checks in terminal build 6230 on one model. It is a StandardScaler followed by a RandomForestClassifier, trained on EURUSD H1 features computed from the terminal's own indicators. The Python package versions are listed in Limitations. The test script runs 36 checks. On all 2,033 golden rows the terminal matched onnxruntime within 1.49e-7. A model retrained with another seed has the same signature and a different hash, and it changes 241 labels on the golden rows. In the Strategy Tester the EA runs both checks in OnInit and then predicts every bar of a later period. Only the first of those bars is also in the golden file. A Python audit of its log found the same labels as onnxruntime and probabilities within 1.49e-7. The model itself is only the test case. It has no edge, and the article does not evaluate it as a strategy.
What is already published
MetaQuotes' article
How to use ONNX models in MQL5
prints the type information of every input and output with
OnnxGetInputTypeInfo()
and
OnnxGetOutputTypeInfo()
. It sets the output shapes by hand.
Classification models in the Scikit-Learn library and their export to ONNX
exports classifiers with the default ZipMap output and reads the resulting sequence of maps in MQL5. It then compares the accuracy on the Iris set in Python and in MQL5.
From Matrices to Models
and
Wasserstein Distance for Live Feature-Drift Detection
put the scaler inside the ONNX graph, and the second one also watches the live distribution of the inputs.
Pipelines in MQL5
does the preprocessing in MQL5 itself.
I found no article that checks a model file against a fixed contract before the EA trades, or compares the terminal's probabilities with Python row by row. Both gaps matter. Accuracy on a whole dataset can match while single rows differ, and a retrained model can have exactly the same signature as the old one.
Architecture
The module consists of four include files, two MQL5 scripts, one EA, and three Python scripts. Fig. 1 shows how the files from the export side reach the checks, and how the EA's log is checked after a Strategy Tester run.
From the export script to the EA
The model, its contract, and the golden rows are checked before the first prediction
Fig. 1. The export script or make_check_files.py writes the model, the contract, the golden rows, and the trees. The contract check, the classifier, and the parity run sit between them and the EA. After a Strategy Tester run, the EA log is audited in onnxruntime and rechecked with a standard-library script

Section 1: The export side
The example features come from ExportFeatures.mq5, which uses the same COnnxFeatures class as the EA. They are the 14-period RSI, the 14-period ATR divided by the close, the 10-bar return, and the width of the 20-period Bollinger Bands divided by the close. The label looks six bars ahead. A return above half the ATR of the bar is class 2, below minus half the ATR is class 0, and anything in between is class 1. ExportFeatures.mq5 also writes the high, low, and close of every bar, so that Section 9 can recompute the features without MQL5.
The script export_model.py splits the rows by time into three parts:

The table dates are the script parameters, compared with the text of the time column. A row belongs to the golden file when 2026.01.01 <= time < 2026.05.01. My MetaQuotes-Demo data has no H1 bars on New Year's Day. The bar after 2025.12.31 23:00 is 2026.01.02 00:00. So the first golden row is 2026.01.02 00:00, and the last golden row is 2026.04.30 23:00. The six-row gap removes training rows only, never golden rows. Data from another server can give a different row count for the same dates.
Without the six-row gap the last training rows would carry information from the first golden bars into the model. That does not change any parity result, but it could make the accuracy below look better than it is. On the golden rows the model's accuracy is 34.7%, below the 37.2% share of the largest class. The model has no edge, and nothing in the checks depends on it having one.
The script fits a StandardScaler and a RandomForestClassifier in one Pipeline and converts it with skl2onnx. The default conversion of a classifier ends in a ZipMap node, so the probability output is a sequence of maps from class to probability. The classes row lists the class labels in the order of the probability columns. The contract check compares their count with the width of the probability output. The label values themselves can only be checked when the model answers, so Predict() refuses any label that is not in this list.
The sha256 row holds the hash of model.onnx.
The script then writes golden.csv with the four features of every golden row. Each row also holds the label and probabilities from onnxruntime and from scikit-learn. A third file, forest.json, holds the scaler and every tree as plain numbers for the check in Section 9. Section 2: Checking the contract
A check ends with one code:
//+------------------------------------------------------------------+
//| Result of a contract check. OK is 0. Among the other codes a     |
//| smaller value is a more serious problem, and when a check finds  |
//| several problems the smallest code becomes the result            |
//+------------------------------------------------------------------+
enum
ENUM_ONNX_CHECK
  {
   ONNX_CHECK_OK=
0
,
// the model matches the contract
ONNX_CHECK_NO_MODEL,
// the model handle is invalid
ONNX_CHECK_NO_CONTRACT,
// the contract is missing, empty or inconsistent
ONNX_CHECK_INPUT_COUNT,
// the model has a different number of inputs
ONNX_CHECK_OUTPUT_COUNT,
// the model has a different number of outputs
ONNX_CHECK_NOT_TENSOR,
// a value is a sequence or a map, not a tensor
ONNX_CHECK_ELEM_TYPE,
// a tensor has a different element type
ONNX_CHECK_SHAPE,
// a dimension differs, or a non-batch dimension is free
ONNX_CHECK_HASH,
// the signature matches, the file is not the one in the contract
ONNX_CHECK_NAME
// a name differs (a problem only in strict mode)
};
ONNX_CHECK_OK is 0. Among the other codes, a smaller value is a more serious problem. A check does not stop at the first problem. It records every problem it finds, and the smallest code becomes the result. Problem() does this, and it is also where a name difference is set aside unless strict mode is on:

//| Record a problem. A name problem changes the result only in      |

The counts come first in the code because OnnxRun() binds its buffers by position. A model with one output fewer does not fail on a name. The mismatch shows up in the first OnnxRun() call, as it did in my first version. Because the smallest code wins, the order of the calls inside Check() does not change the result. A ZipMap model checked in strict mode has three problems at once (a sequence output, a different label name, and a different hash), and the result is ONNX_CHECK_NOT_TENSOR. Test 15 in Section 6 checks exactly this.
Dimension 0 is treated as the batch, and a free size there matches any size. Every other dimension must be fixed and equal on both sides. A model with a free feature or class dimension fails with ONNX_CHECK_SHAPE. This is a deliberate restriction. COnnxClassifier needs those sizes to build its buffers, and a model whose dimension 0 is not a batch does not fit this class at all.
The hash compares the bytes the session was created from with the sha256 row. A model with the same signature and other weights passes every other test in Check() and fails this one. When a check fails, Signature() returns what the model reports, one value per line, and the hash of its bytes.
A name difference is always listed, but it fails the check only when SetStrictNames(true) is set. OnnxRun() takes the buffers by position and does not use the names, and skl2onnx changes them with its options ("output_label" with ZipMap, "label" without it).
Section 3: The classifier
COnnxClassifier owns the session. LoadFile() reads the model as bytes and creates the session with OnnxCreateFromBuffer(), so the hash covers exactly what the session runs. ONNX_NO_CONVERSION
. Without it the terminal converts the input data automatically, and the contract has already fixed the input as float. ClassIndex() maps a label to its probability column through the classes row. Each call is timed with GetMicrosecondCount(), and Latency() returns the median, the 99th percentile, and the maximum.
Section 4: The golden file
COnnxParity::Run() finds every column by its name. The feature columns come from the features row of the contract. The answer columns are ort_label, ort_p0, ort_p1, and so on. The scikit-learn columns skl_label and skl_p0 onwards are optional. Every row goes through Predict(). The largest difference to each Python answer is kept, and every row over the tolerance can be written to a file for inspection:
//+------------------------------------------------------------------+
//| Run every golden row and compare with the Python answers. Every  |

To confirm that the tests can fail, I introduced three defects into the classes, one per copy, and ran the test script on each defective copy. In the first copy, Run() ignored the probability difference and compared only the labels. The golden file with one probability moved by 0.01 then passed. Check 30 expects that file to fail, so check 30 reported FAIL. In the second copy, Check() skipped the output count. Checks 6 and 25 on the model without its probability output reported FAIL, because the result became ONNX_CHECK_HASH instead of ONNX_CHECK_OUTPUT_COUNT. In the third copy, Check() skipped the hash. Checks 7, 12, 15, and 27 reported FAIL, and the retrained model loaded without complaint. Each defect was found, and the code was restored.

Section 9: A consistency check outside MQL5
When one implementation both produces and checks the numbers, the same error can pass both steps. The script parity_crosscheck.py uses only the Python 3 standard library. It is my second implementation of the same model and feature formulas, so I call it a consistency check. It does not replace a check by someone else. It reads forest.json and walks every tree itself, in two ways. The sklearn walk scales in float32 as (x - mean) / scale and compares with the float64 thresholds. The onnx walk scales as (x - mean) * (1 / scale) in float32. It compares with each threshold replaced by the largest float32 that is not above it, because skl2onnx writes the graph that way. A third walk, onnx-nearest, rounds the thresholds to the nearest float32 instead. It then compares both walks with the golden file and the EA log, and recomputes the four features from the price data in features.csv:

Both walks reproduce scikit-learn within 1.11e-16 and onnxruntime within 5.79e-8 on the golden rows, and they reach the same leaf on every golden row. On the 2,592 bars of the tester run, the onnx walk matches the probabilities the EA logged within 1.26e-7. The line for the onnx-nearest walk shows an assumption of mine that was wrong. An earlier version of my onnx walk rounded every threshold to the nearest float32. It disagreed with the EA by 0.00195 on one bar, 2026.09.28 09:00. On that bar, tree 36 splits on atr14_norm at node 10, and the scaled value is exactly the nearest float32 of the threshold. skl2onnx did not store that value in this export. The export output in Section 1 shows that skl2onnx stored all 2,335 split thresholds as the largest float32 value that does not exceed the float64 threshold. For 582 of them, this value differs from the nearest float32. For a float32 input, x <= that value holds exactly when x <= the float64 threshold. So for a float32 input the graph takes the same branch as scikit-learn, and only my wrong walk went the other way.

Она посвящена инфраструктуре верификации корректности выполнения ONNX-моделей в MQL5: проверке контракта (соответствие входов/выходов, хеша, типов данных), золотого файла (сравнение предсказаний терминала с onnxruntime по фиксированному набору строк) и классификатора. В тексте отсутствуют: направление входа (long/short), условия входа, параметры сигнала, логика генерации торговых решений — всё это является фатальным пороком для требования 'чётко описанное условие входа с параметрами и их значениями'. Статья про тестирование и достоверность вычислений, а не про правило торговли.
judge.summary: Статья представляет методы верификации корректности работы ONNX-моделей в MQL5: проверку контракта, золотой файл для сравнения предсказаний с onnxruntime и хеш-валидацию. Она демонстрирует, что терминал выдаёт те же метки и вероятности, что и Python, с точностью до 1.49e-7 на 2033 барах. Однако статья не содержит ни одного торгового правила, сигнала, условия входа или выхода — её цель исключительно обеспечение надёжности инференса ML-моделей в среде MetaTrader.
